utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We can begin the session by talking about interpretation and listening to each other. First of all, Prosecutor, can you hear what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Registrar, can you as well? The interpreters can communicate with each other? Our colleagues? The legal assistants? Good. So we can begin the session. Prosecuting counsel, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Before I call the first witness, there is a brief preliminary matter. At this time I would like to tender to the court exhibits 15 through 22 which are the computer maps that were displayed on the first day. We have now obtained hard copy print-outs of these so at this time I will submit these to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Registrar, would you take possession of those maps? (Handed)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, your Honour, we are ready to call the first witness, Dr. Jan Schou.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Jan Schou.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please show Dr. Schou in. DR. JAN SCHOU, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Schou, would you mind standing up again, please? If the usher could ask the witness to stand up again, please? Doctor, would you mind standing up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to speak English.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Schou, the judge was just asking you to stand up, please. Thank you very much. Would you be kind to introduce yourself to the Tribunal? Your family name, your first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my first name is Jan Schou and I am a medical doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read out the solemn declaration which the usher is going to give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, please be seated. I did not actually hear that. Fine, that is fine. OK. Please be seated. No problem, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Dr. Schou, you indicated that you are physician; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I am what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: A doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long have you been a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For 10 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you have a field of specialisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am a surgeon and a gynaecologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Prior to going into medicine did you spend a period of time in the Danish Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am educated as an officer in reserve in the Danish Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you serve in active service with the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In the early part of 1991 where were you working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working on hospital in Jutland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is in Denmark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Denmark, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At some point in 1991 did you become affiliated with the European Community Monitoring Mission, with the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was called at the hospital from the Danish military that asked me to go to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When did this occur, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It occurred -- just a moment -- it occurred Thursday, 10th October 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were the circumstances under which you went to work for the ECMM? What did the Danish military ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They need a military person that also was a doctor, not a military doctor but a military person that was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: OK. Did you, in fact, go to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went on Tuesday 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where exactly did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I go to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you arrived in Zagreb were you given a particular assignment by the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did the ECMM ask you to do when you arrived in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me to be the doctor for the EC member and then to be the EC medical doctor in all aspect about human right, the prisoners and wounded and something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: OK. Did you participate in a relief convoy that was going to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When did this convoy depart from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about Friday 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did it take you to reach Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It take one day to reach just outside Vukovar to the borderline and then we sleep there the night over and the next day, the next morning, at 6 o'clock, we start the evacuation to cross borderline with the Medicines without Border.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time was fighting still going on in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So this was not going on at the time of the fall of the City; this was approximately a month before that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a month before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: OK. What did you observe when you entered into Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I observed a really damaged city and there has been heavy shelling in the city, and most of the building were damaged. But we only went to the hospital. We did not travel around in the city. We only went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you arrived at the hospital what condition was it in at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hospital was one of the most damaged building. It was only the basement that could be used. Everything else was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In all how long were you in the hospital that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we were there at 10 o'clock, or something like, and then we leave with the wounded about 3 o'clock in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Approximately how many patients in your estimation were in the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about, if you only talk about patient, I think there must be about 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How many patients were you able to take out in the relief convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We take 107 of the most wounded or 104, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you able to observe the working conditions at that time for the doctors and the other medical staff in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they work with, they were doing a good job with the few things they had to do it with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did they have an adequate supply of medicine and bandages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not have anything. They have to use the supply again and again. They have to wash the bandage and something like that and use it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After you were able to get the patients out for the return to Zagreb, did you follow the same route as you had on the way into Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the way into Vukovar, we had changed the road due to the Croatians said that this was a better way, and we reached the hospital, of course. On the way out we tried to went out the same way, but there must have been some on the road because there was a wire across the road and just after that we were not attacked but stopped by the JNA Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In fact, you were stopped by a JNA tank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was stopped by a JNA tank, yes, and I was in the front car. I was in the leading on the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The tank gun barrel was pointed at your car, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, and we had to jump out of the car while it was still running.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who was the JNA officer in command at this blockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We think that it was the Colonel, as I think he was at that time, I heard his name was Sljivanovic (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sljivancanin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did he tell you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had arranged a press conference at the top of a hill. At that time we were stopped. There was a lot of television from Belgrade, from ITV and something like that. I think there was about three or four different television crew at the top of the hill. Then he had a press conference where he declare that we were not following the agreement, that we take not only wounded but also soldiers out in the car and that -----

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did he give you any instructions about what you were to do from that point on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said we should follow the original agreement and that we should follow the road to the next city which we not follow on the way out because the Croatians said it was mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you indicate to him that you were concerned about this fact, that the road might be mined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we said that the road was, we were told that the road was mined, and we did not want to drive that way, but he said we were not allowed to go any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, go on the road that Major Sljivancanin directed you to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The result was that No. 4 car went on into a mine on the road and were blowing up and two nurses from, I think it was, Switzerland were thrown out of the car and hit the ground, and I and some of the staff from the Medicine Without Border, we had to treat them and at that time we get also help from the JNA Army and they have a helicopter so they can fly the two wounded nurses to the hospital in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did these nurses survive the explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they survived, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where they seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time we could not see if they were seriously wounded. We could see one of them had a broken leg and they were bleeding from the ears, but later I heard that they were deaf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: They lost their hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They lost their hearing, both, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This occurred on the road Major Sljivancanin had ordered you to go on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After the explosion did you see Major Sljivancanin again that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In November were you asked to return to Vukovar once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the reason for this trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason was I was in Zagreb at that time and we had a negotiation with General Raseta about the evacuation of Vukovar one time more, and then we suddenly heard that Vukovar was nearly taken, and then I went to Belgrade together with the head of Mission and from Belgrade we tried to make an arrangement with the Red Cross to get the wounded out, but we did not reach it because we heard that the city was almost taken, so it was impossible to get in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you eventually go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I go with, we were two EC team, EC member team, and then I with a command of this evacuation or observation, if you can say so, and then we have two relief, what do you call that, relief officers from the Headquarters in the Military Headquarters in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On what date did you arrive in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived the 19th of November in the morning. In the morning we reach the area of Vukovar but we were not allowed to go to the area of Vukovar. We were staying outside a city called Sid for maybe four or five hours, waiting for permission to go to the operation area and then we went to the operation area in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you eventually go to Negaslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We go to Negaslavci, to the Headquarter of the Military Army forces in that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who did you meet with in Negaslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we meet Sljivanci (sic) ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- Sljivancanin again, but at this time he was a Major. Later we had met him, when I had met him, he was a Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you say anything to him about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and he said he always had been a Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were your impressions of Major Sljivancanin in terms of what he was doing with the Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he is a kind of political officer, and why I think it is because I am educated in intelligence in the Danish Army, and he had, he wear new, quite new uniform and all other people, including the General, and something like that, they used clothes that you could see had been used, through exposed to the sun and the underground and something like that. But he had a quite new uniform and, even if he spoke with some superior officer, I could feel that he was in command, even if he only was a Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this meeting with Major Sljivancanin was Colonel Mrksic also present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you and your associate from the ECMM attempt to get access to Vukovar Hospital on that day, on 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 19th, we tried to get to Vukovar because we had heard that the hospital were taken, or nearly were taken, and we want to go to the hospital and at that time we make a connection with our phone with Dr. Bosanac in Vukovar, and she nearly cry that we had to come as soon as possible because they were doing some awful things in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you able to get to the hospital on 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Major Sljivancanin, he said that we were not allowed to go the hospital due to our secure, but at the same time we hear from the Red Cross that they had reached the hospital without no problem and they were throwing away from the hospital by the soldiers, and I think that the Major himself went to the hospital and took the Red Cross out because he come back later that evening and said that the Red Cross, that they could not trust the Red Cross because they did not follow any agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The Red Cross had, in fact, made it to the hospital safely ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: -- on 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But was thrown out by Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and we also heard that night from Major Sljivancanin that they have taken over the hospital and that they have removed Dr. Bosanac and some other Ustasha from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the course of the evening of 19th were any arrangements made for you to go into the hospital the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was meaning that we the next morning, that I could go to the hospital with my interpreter which was Peter Kypr and only, and only the two of us could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The following morning, on 20th November, did your team attempt to go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have a secure of military soldiers and we went to the middle of the town just where the River ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Vuka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- Vuka go through the city and at that point we were stopped and hold back for about two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who stopped you at the bridge over the Vuka River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Physically, it was a tank on the bridge that were, not a tank -- what do you call it -- a personnel car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: An armoured personnel carrier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A personnel car, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Or an APC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An APC, yes. It was on the bridge and then Major Sljivancanin was at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At approximately what time in the morning was it that you arrived on this bridge, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it must be about 9 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So it was fairly early on the morning of 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did Major Sljivancanin tell you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He tell us that due to our security we were not able to go to the hospital. They had to clean the road before we go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you what the danger was for you moving any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The danger, it was that there still were some fighting going on and there could be snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you able to see down the street from the Vuka River bridge in the direction of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see any signs of fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see any people walking in the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did any of them appear to be taking cover or any other kind of defensive measures, being concerned about snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you hear any gunfire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a few, and also just beneath us there were soldiers that were firing in the air just for fun, and they were, most of the soldiers at that time, it was what I called Chetnik and they were drunken. They were firing that they had taken the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So the only gunfire that you heard seemed to be in celebration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The distance to the hospital from the bridge was relatively short, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about one and a half, two kilometres, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: OK. Were you present when the representative from the International Red Cross tried to get past Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was at the bridge at the same time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The member from the Red Cross, he started shouting with Major Sljivancanin, but he did not argument; they just shouted each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But Major Sljivancanin would not let him pass either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At that time he also told the other that I was responsible for the evacuation of the hospital, it was that Red Cross was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you eventually allowed to pass through and go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about two hours we went to the hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show the witness a brief clip of video from the exhibit previously marked as exhibit 23. Do you recognise this location here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you see a picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If we can stop it and start again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is nothing on the video, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now if you can start it? (The video was played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, now I see. I can see the car, the bridge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This is the bridge over the Vuka River where you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes and that is the Red Cross that arrived and that the chief of the Red Cross and that, of course, Major Sljivancanin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This is the new uniform that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As opposed to the uniforms of everyone else around him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What is going on at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They discuss or argument, or what you can call it, about why we were not allowed to go and why the Red Cross not could go because Red Cross could go everywhere in the world but not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The Red Cross representative was pointing out that people were moving freely and there seemed to be no problem in moving down the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yet Major Sljivancanin still refused to allow you through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see in the picture, there are no fighting in the area beneath the car; you can see everyone just walked around; there is no snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If you were in a situation of combat, based on your military experience, and there were snipers and there was fighting going on, would you be walking around bare-headed or would you wear a helmet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would wear a flack jacket -- not a helmet, I do not think it helped anyway. But I think it is that time that the Major tells that, "I am in command", or in command; we were not allowed to do anything. We were just allowed to watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where were you located when this was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were located just to the left of the Red Cross car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is this your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not my vehicle. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is this you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is me and Peter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: OK. This is when you were first entering the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This is you on the left, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was going on at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the time he told that, "It is only me that could make decision", and he also told that the JNA Army would manage the evacuation and we had to watch it and the Red Cross has to follow what the EC member say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now if we can move forward to the next clip, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you like to pose any more questions, Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want him to identify one other thing, it will be very brief, and then I can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, it is just that I was not hearing anything and I was not sure if there was another technical problem or whether you had finished. Excuse me for interrupting. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Do you recognise this location that is portrayed here in the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the headquarter in Negaslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who is the gentleman in the military uniform next to Cyrus Vance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the Colonel and that is chief of the whole operation in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That was Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his name you told me, but I recognise him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is all that we need to see of the video. Thank you. When you arrived at the hospital, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I observed that they were walking Chetniks around in the hospital together with the wounded, and some of the Chetniks were beating the wounded, both with their guns and with their boots, and there were only bad wounded men, no men at all -- there were only bad wounded men, men that would probably die in a few days or something like that, and then old men and small kids and women, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see any men that appeared to be of fighting age who were lightly wounded or not wounded at all in the area of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some bad wounded at the fighting age, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But none that were lightly wounded ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: -- or not wounded at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only some of the people, because the Red Cross make a list and asked the people whether they want to go to Serbia or whether they want to go to Croatia after the evacuation, and some of the people that want to go to Serbia, they were, you can see, in the middle age, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see any men that appeared to have been recently wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Recent?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Wounded in the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, all the people in the hospital, they were wounded at least one hour before -- one week before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you think that this was unusual since there had been fighting going on in the city, according to Major Sljivancanin, up until an hour ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if there had been fighting going on, there must have been some wounded from the last day or last two days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the course of the day, were you or Peter Kypr given any information on what had happened to all of the male patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only heard that I told you before, that Dr. Bosanac and some of the Ustashas were taken away the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did anyone say what had happened to the other male patients in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you able eventually to evacuate some of the patients from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, JNA military -- a JNA unit, hospital unit, made the evacuation of some of the wounded in the 20s and some of the wounded in the 21s.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where were these patients taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken to near a military infirmary in -- I cannot remember the name of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It was a city in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a city in Serbia beneath the border to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: From there where were the patients taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From there, the next day the patients were taken to Bronk, I think it was, the name was, in Bosnia just at the, across the borderline, and there it was planned to take the patients from the Serbian vehicles to a Croatian vehicles, but in that area we met a lot of violence from the local, so we had to move to another town to make that change vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The violence that you encountered was from local Serbs in the Bosnian town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Local Serbs in the Bosnian town, yes, and also the EC members were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: They attacked the EC members as well as the patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were there Army soldiers or Police present when this was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did the convoy eventually make it safely back to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It went not to Zagreb, it went through Bosnia and then it went up to, I think about, Vinkovci, or something like that, a hospital there where it was arranged that we should reach, and then we leave the convoy and the Croatian take over the wounded and we follow the road back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel for the Prosecutor. Judge Odio Benito?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Just a small question: Doctor, could you tell me again the exact date the first time you went to Vukovar because I missed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first day I went to Vukovar was in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In October, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19/20th of October, it was at first Vukovar where I get the wounded out with the Medicine without Border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like you to give us some more information about what you have said to the Tribunal. You said that at the hospital the Chetniks were beating injured people. Could you give us maybe a bit more detail about that? I think it does deserve a little bit more information, in particular, you did refer to those who were particularly seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers were -- the wounded were laying on the floor in the basement and these Serbian soldiers or the Chetniks, they were walking around with two or three persons together everywhere, and then they went to the soldiers -- to the wounded and just kick at them and something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I suppose that this must have been a terrible scene to witness. How did the representatives of the Red Cross react? Did they do anything? Did they try to stop it? Was Commander Sljivancanin present at the scene? Did the leaders in the Red Cross delegation try to do something? Was there a manager from the hospital? Although Dr. Bosanac was not there, was there another manager from the hospital who was present, because it would appear to be quite intolerable that in the company of the Red Cross this beating should be taking place in the hospital. What is your general impression of what took place during this scene, as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that the command of the hospital at that time was a Serbian military doctor or doctors. I think there were four or five of them. They wear uniforms and they were really drunken at that time. Of course, both Red Cross and the EC member, we claim that the patient were treated, but as they always said: "It was only Ustasha". So then we had -- I talk with my secure, which was the Military Police from the real Army, real JNA Army, and they help us to get all these Chetniks out of the hospital so we could start the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, doctor. The Tribunal would like to thank you for your testimony. The counsel for the Prosecution has no further questions, so we would like to bring your testimony to a close and show you out to the room which has been reserved for you as a witness. If the usher could help with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I now call Dr. Snow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, it seems to be a very long road for the witness to get to the court room! I wonder whether the witness is ready because, if not, maybe we should adjourn. In fact, we were planning to adjourn at around 11 o'clock or 11.15 anyway. Registrar, what do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the situation with witnesses is something I do not know because it is being handled by another organisation of the Tribunal, so where they are or what is happening, I am afraid I cannot assist, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, please do not misunderstand me. I did not mean to reproach you in any way whatsoever. I am sure both of us were wondering about what was happening. I felt that if the witness was not going to be able to come in a short period that we should say that to the Tribunal so that the Tribunal could adopt some relevant measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if your Honours wish to take an adjournment now, that is certainly no problem as far as I am concerned. DR. CLYDE SNOW, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough to put the headphones on? The usher will help you. Usher, would you please ask the witness to remain standing before the Tribunal? Thank you very much, sir. We would like you to remain standing just for a few seconds. Firstly, could you put your headphones on -- thank you very much, thank you, doctor -- then you can hear what we are saying to you. Doctor, can you hear what I am saying to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Would you be kind enough to introduce yourself, your family name and your first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Clyde Snow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please pick up the solemn declaration which the usher is going to give to you and read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, doctor. Please make yourself comfortable, doctor. You have been requested to appear by the Prosecution and so the Prosecutor will have some questions for you which he feels important, and perhaps the Tribunal will also have some additional questions to add to its information for you as well. Prosecuting counsel, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, you were born in Fort Worth, Texas, in the United States of America?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You hold an Associate of Arts from the New Mexico Military Institute; a Bachelor of Science from the Eastern New Mexico University; a Master of Science from the Texas Technical University; a Doctor of Philosophy from the University of Arizona and a Doctor of Science (Honours) from John Jay College of Criminal Justice which you got in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You had a career initially with the Federal Aviation Administration in the United States of America?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then during your career you have served as a consultant in some 3,000 cases involving the identification and determination of a cause of death of skeletonised victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your cases have included a 1979 American Airlines DC10 crash in Chicago which involved the death of some 273 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1985 at the request of the Simon Wiesenthal Institute you headed a team of US Forensic Scientists which went to Brazil in order to carry out an identification on the Nazi war criminal, Dr. Jozef Mengele?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1984, under the sponsorship of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, you went to Argentina to serve as a Consultant to that Nation's National Commission on Disappeared Persons in an effort to determine the fate of thousands of Argentinians who had been abducted and tortured during the period 1976 to 1983?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1992 you served in Geneva as the United States delegate to the United Nations Human Rights Commission, and you also completed several United Nations sponsored missions to the former Yugoslavia to collect forensic evidence to be used in proceedings before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, have you held approximately six university appointments throughout your career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you been involved with approximately 12 consultantships?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you a member of 10 professional organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you been awarded and honoured on at least 24 occasions for the work that you have been carrying out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you organised and participated and directed in at least nine courses in relation to forensic science and the work in which you are involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you published or participated in the publication of in excess of 90 publications, be it articles through to books, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, were you requested during the year 1992 to participate in the exhumation of suspected mass graves in the Vukovar area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was a member of the Mazowiecki Commission which went to Yugoslavia with, and one aspect of that Commission's mandate was to investigate allegations of mass graves and other atrocities that had occurred in former Yugoslavia. One of those cases happened to be the disappearance of the roughly 250 or so people from the hospital in Vukovar, hospital patients and staff, in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Tribunal what you did, in particular, with respect to this mass grave site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, may I refer to my notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means, with your Honours' leave, I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, if you like, Mr. Prosecutor, I could more or less describe out my activities with the Mazowiecki Commission and later investigations more or less chronologically?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, if you would, please, go through. I think in the course of the explanation you will give in relation to what you observed and did at Vukovar, you will throughout giving testimony wish to refer to a number of slides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Those slides that you will refer to will roughly follow a chronological approach to the presentation of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think, in addition to that, there is also a map that you might refer us to in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of the giving of your evidence, if you would just indicate to us in advance when it is that you wish to refer to them, then arrangements can be made for it to be displayed on the overhead video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I believe that if we could bring this unit around ... The Mazowiecki Commission, we arrived in Zagreb on October 12th 1992. On October 14th I had a conference with Dr. Ivica Kostovic, who at that time was the Dean of the Medical Faculty and also the head of a joint commission that had been established to locate missing persons and repatriate the remains of people who had been killed during the hostilities. Meeting with him at the Faculty of Medicine that morning, we reviewed several cases, but one that he described to me that struck me as being particularly interesting and worth pursuing was the incident involving the disappearance of the patients and the medical staff from the hospital in Vukovar in, I believe it was, November 20th 1991. In our conversation he provided me first with a map of the general area, which I will refer to here a little later, and he also mentioned a witness which I believe you referred to in these proceedings as "Witness B".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that Witness B had some detailed information about the disappearances at Vukovar. I asked if I might meet with the witness and, through intermediaries, he was able to contact Witness B and we made arrangements for him to, for me to interview him. Witness B arrived at my room, room 1405, at approximately 6 p.m. on the evening of October 15th. I was -- in the room, my room at that time, with Dr. Jack Geiger, Miss Lindsay Cook, both of him were also members of the Mazowiecki Commission and a translator who took notes, translated and transcribed my interview, Mr. Thomas Osorio. Prior to that time I had been provided with a statement that Witness B had given to Dr. Kostovic's Commission in August of 1992. I had gone over that. So, in my interview I wanted to take him through his experience there as he described it in as much detail as I could, and to see if his story was, you know, always consistent with what he had already given. Once we introduced ourselves and made ourselves comfortable, I asked him to simply start out and describe his whole experience. Then later I would come back and ask him more detailed questions. He did. He described his going to the hospital that morning, being loaded on to buses, taken first to the JNA barracks close to Vukovar there. I will not go into details because I believe he has already testified to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then later into a hangar situated near Ovcara where they spent several hours being brutalised by, apparently, military and paramilitary Serbian people who had taken them there. Then around 6 p.m., somewhere after dark -- he was not sure about the time -- they started breaking the men up in the barracks into groups of around 20 and a truck would come and they would load these groups, 20, roughly 20 men at a time, on to the trucks, on to the truck, and the truck would disappear and it would come back about, he estimated, 10 to 15 minutes later, empty and they would take another group of 20 or so prisoners. He noted to me that it was always the same truck, and so he figured that the round trip was in the neighbourhood of, to wherever they were taking these prisoners, was within a 15 minute round trip or so. So it could not be too far from the farm there at Ovcara. When it came to his turn in the group he was in and, as I recall, he could not be sure whether he was in the third or the fourth truck load, but he boarded the truck, he said that it went -- it took the road toward, from Ovcara down to another village or farm called Grabovo, and then after a few minutes though, it turned off this paved road to the left and entered a farm road or just a dirt track, that was skirted on one side he could see timber trees and on his right as the truck was proceeding and on the left open fields. He became very apprehensive and he managed, he decided that he would try to escape and he jumped out of the truck while it was in motion after it had entered a field for a distance of roughly 200 to 300 metres, he estimated. When he jumped from the truck it was dark, although there was a moon out, conditions were dry and he started running. He did not -- he thought about running into the woods on his right, but he decided to run across the open field towards Vukovar. As he was running, he could hear the truck continue on. It continued for a short distance and then he heard, as I recall -- I would have to look at his statement detail -- he heard the truck stop and then he heard a few shots. He continued running into Vukovar where later he was taken prisoner by JNA forces and repatriated after a few months in prison. So that was his experience. Now, I was trying to evaluate the witness. I am not a professional interrogator, but I was trying to get a sense of how reliable he was. First, he struck me as a pretty straightforward young man, who was telling a straightforward story, and I was struck by the fact that, like in other cases where I have been involved, witnesses sometimes either through faulty memory or they exaggerate a little bit, they make things a little more lurid then they actually are, and such details as, for example, when he jumped from the truck and when he heard those shots, I asked him: "You know, well, was that enough? Did you hear enough gunfire to account for the execution of whole truck load of men?" And he said: "No", he said, "you know, there was only five or six shots", and his theory was that maybe one other passenger had tried to jump out of the truck after he did, and at this time they noticed it and they were firing to, perhaps, bring him down. But he did not, you know, I would have been a little more suspicious if he had told me that he had heard lots of gunfire and lots of, you know, screaming and things of that sort. He said, no, he just kept running and that was all he heard. His story ended there. Now, can we set this -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you like to refer to a document now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have the map here, the original map that was given to me by Dr. Kostovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, we have now made a hard copy of that map. If we use that copy, we can then tender it and that will become exhibit 28, if your Honours please? You might just -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You do not mind if I turn away here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, you should be able to be heard. You might just orientate everything on the map for us, if you would, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. This map -- that is fine right there -- this is the farm at Ovcara. Now this map is dated 1973. It is a topographical survey that was done by the Yugoslavian authorities. I am not sure whether it shows the building that -- it may not have been built in 1973 -- the men were taken to first, but it would be along this road right about where my finger is, here. The road that the Witness B said that they left in the truck passes down here toward this village of Grabovo. He and I looked at this map over there in the room in Zagreb. He is an engineer. He was an officer in the Croatian forces and before that, the JNA reserve. So, he is familiar with topographical maps. We were looking at it and, from the time and distances he described, the only place it would physically correspond to his description of being a short distance from Ovcara, turning off to the left into a field bounded on the right by woods, on the left by open fields, would be this ravine which cuts across this road almost exactly one kilometre from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The ravine is shown as the darker green area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the green area running up this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The woods followed somewhere along that route as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the ravine itself is wooded heavy and the road paralleled that ravine, not in the woods but at the edge of the woods and at the edge of the field on one side and the woods on the other. He felt like he made his jump, as I said, 200 to 300 metres into the field. He and I looked at the map and I had -- this road, no, it goes nowhere, it ends along in here. There is no other facility or any structures in that field, so it is an empty field. Based on my experiences being raised in Texas and Oklahoma, ranchers and farmers, if we have a ravine like this on your place, you would figure that the head of the ravine ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might point to it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the head of the ravine, we always considered those kind of waste areas. So I talked to Witness B and we, kind of, agreed that if there were a mass grave, they probably would not be putting it out in the field that would be used ordinarily for agricultural purposes; they would probably place it somewhere close to the head of that ravine which, as I indicated, at least where I come from, that is considered a kind of waste land. In fact, very often farmers and ranchers will use the head because a ravine like this is apt to cause a lot of erosion of soil. They usually will throw crash, debris, things of that sort, in there to help to control the erosion. But, at any rate, I said, and Witness B and I agreed, that probably if there was a mass grave, if the executions had occurred in this area, it would be rather close to the head of this ravine. I happen to put a little point on the map there. I drew a wider circle saying, "Well, yes, surely, it would be, most likely be, in this area".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, you did this before you visited the scene? You drew the circle and put the dot there before you visited the scene and during the course of your conversation with Witness B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was the evening of October 15th in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At that stage you had not visited the scene at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The circle that you see there is the original circle that you put on the map during the course of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So armed with this map, and at the request of the people or the head of the Mazowiecki Commission, I went to Vukovar arriving there through Belgrade. I flew to Belgrade and then surface transportation from Belgrade to Vukovar; arrived there in the evening or early afternoon of October 17th. There I met a Royal Canadian mounted Police sergeant who was with the CIVPOL unit there in Vukovar, whose name was staff sergeant Larry Moore. I showed him this map. He was quite familiar with the area. By that time I believe he had been based there in Vukovar for several months. So the next morning we proceeded out to this area and, because of road conditions, we parked our vehicles right at the intersection or close to the bridge where this ravine crosses the Ovcara Gravobo road. We were accompanied by Colonel Peters, then Colonel now General Peters, of the Belgian battalion there in Sector East, by Ms. Vlandina Nega who was a UN civil affairs officer, and one of Colonel Peters' officers or staff members. We left our translators in the car but we walked on up the ravine more or less following the road here on the left side of the ravine. Sergeant Moore was ahead of us. He was walking faster. I told him that what you would look for in the way of a mass grave like this would be some kind of disturbance of the vegetation, maybe a new, you know, a new generation of vegetation coming in, we see or just open space or -- so he knew what to look for. He walking faster got, as I recall, a couple of hundred metres ahead of Ms. Vlandina Nega and I. Once he got up to this point, I heard him, I saw him motioning and calling out. He had found something rather suspicious. So we hurried up there and now I would like to show some slides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will tender that map, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to keep that map handy though because I may be wanting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I will tender it at the end of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the lights might be dimmed, if your Honours please, so that it might make it a bit more obvious. Could the lights be dimmed a little, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I caught up with Sergeant Moore he was standing at the edge of this open area that he had found right at the head of the ravine. You can see it is surrounded by a low growth of weeds that were only about a year old compared to older bushes and shrubs and small saplings a little beyond this area. In fact, the centre of the area had very little vegetation on it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who is this standing in the photograph there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Sergeant Moore. This is also, perhaps, a better photograph showing what I was talking about. In this area here you can see a low growth of weeds about waist high, smaller weeds ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you point on the slide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- plants in this area, but a largely open area. It is a spot that, an archeologist would refer to it as a non-functional aspect of the landscape. It is something that should not be there, you know, it is not natural. So this is the kind of thing that arouses our suspicion and we see them in cases of this sort. Now, Sergeant Moore and Colonel Peters and Miss Nega and I proceeded into the area. Sergeant Moore insisted on leading the way in because he was a little concerned with mines, so he walked in through the area and then we followed. Now, in that initial inspection line right there close to the surface was a human skull at one end of that cleared area which I will later refer to, will refer to as skeleton No. 1. It was just incompletely buried. Here is a close-up. Here you can see the orbits or eyehole of the skull itself or the cranial vault. Down here is the jaw, a portion of the tooth there. This is a photograph of the skull as it was more or less exposed in the mud there. I was able to, just based on this initial inspection, I could tell that it was probably, it was a male because of the heavy brow ridges, probably an adult -- well, an adult male, probably a little on the younger side and, most interestingly, over here on the left, in the left temple area, there is a defect or a hole and it is bevelled in such a direction that I can determine that it was an exit wound, that a missile had passed through this skull, exited along this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that missile consistent with a bullet from a -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly is. It is typical. Later on, as we walked through the area walking beyond the grave site, I was able to find another skeleton about 17 metres from the edge of the grave. It was simply lying as it was, whereas this one was partially, still partially buried, this one was lying on the surface and bones had been scattered. It look liked they had been bleached by sun, they were very white, and they showed some marks that animal scavengers had inflicted on them, had damaged them, and there was some clothing. Again this was the skeleton of a young male ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have a photograph of that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- or an adult male. I will have one here a little later that will show some aspects of that. There was some clothing around. My impression was that this individual had not been in this particular mass grave. He may have been executed close to it or he could have been shot, fallen into the grave and then maybe just wounded and had tried to work his way out and crawled behind the area away from the grave and died there. But, anyway, that was a second skeleton that we observed on the site. Now, at this time as we had walked up the ravine to get to this site, there were some men in a -- with a vehicle, wagon and a tractor, as I recall, parked along the wooded area and we could hear -- I do not ever recall seeing the men, but we could hear voices in there and we heard saws, like they were probably cutting wood. But, after talking briefly with, conferring with, Sergeant Moore and Colonel Peters, we decided that if we showed undue attention to this site at that time, that if these people were -- I mean, obviously, they would have been Serbian, probably residents of the farm at Ovcara, the word would get out very rapidly that we had found the grave. So we decided to cut our visit short. We were not there more than, perhaps, 15 minutes on the site. Then we walked back down, got to our vehicles and our concern was that if, for example, word had leaked out and the site was not secured, that it would be very easy, say that night, to come in there, people who would like to destroy that grave, to come in and remove the bodies en masse and perhaps move them to another area or throw them in the Danube, which is no more than, I believe, a mile or so from where this grave is located. So, we were -- in fact, at the scene, I should mention that I was so concerned about this and so was Mr. or Sergeant Moore that around this first skeleton I cleared away some of the bones and exposed the left scapula and we photographed it. We marked it and we photographed it in situ where it was lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might tell us what a scapula is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A scapula is a shoulder blade, the bone back here in the shoulder; in Spanish, homoplato. We took that and I gave it to Sergeant Moore and I told him, you know, to keep custody of this so in case we did come back out and the bodies were gone, that we would at least could say that there were human remains at that site when we first examined it. He took that and put it in, it remained in his custody until I returned to the site in December, the following December. But, at that point we returned back to the UNPROFOR Headquarters at Erdut conferring again with Colonel Peters, and the area happened to fall in the jurisdiction of the Russian battalion. So with the RUSBAT Commander, we talked with him and we insisted or pointed out that it was absolutely necessary that this site be secured as soon as possible and that it be maintained as any other homicide scene. We had evidence of human bodies, some hint of a mass grave and evidence that these people had died of gun shot wounds, so it was a homicide scene. So the RUSBAT Commander made arrangements for a section of Russian troops to go out there and secure the site, the scene. Meanwhile, since that would take a few hours, Sergeant Moore sent a vehicle out with a couple of his own CIVPOL, civilian police, people on his staff, to stay there until they were relieved by the Russians. This was on October 18th. As it turned out, the Russians, there were some confusion as to where the site was located and the Russian group did not arrive there until around 11 p.m. that night. At that time, as I understand it, the CIVPOL policemen left and the Russians took over and secured the scene. There was one other minor problem in that the next morning when we returned to the scene around 10 o'clock, the Russians were gone. They had stayed there. We found out that they had stayed there that night, but it was their understanding that this was just a one-night affair, so they had decamped the next morning. We had to go back and explain to them that we wanted that perimeter established with people out there from that moment on, no matter how long it took. So, they did return and it is my understanding that that scene is still maintained by or secured by Russian troops or Russian detachment. So at that point, on October 20th, I returned to Zagreb. On October 22nd the Mazowiecki Commission met again. We gave a very brief press conference there in Zagreb and mentioned the fact that we had found evidence of a mass grave at the place called, near Ovcara. Later on, on October 27th, a report was issued with a lengthier statement from the Mazowiecki Commission issued in Geneva, and there is a lengthier statement by myself in, what they call it, Annex 2 of that document. On December 17th, I returned with some colleagues of mine, Mr. Eric Stover of Physicians for Human Rights, Dr. Rebecca Sanders, who is an archeologist now with the State of Louisiana, and Dr. Morris Tidball-Binz, who is currently with Amnesty International. We wanted at that point to do what we would call a reconnaissance of the site; not a complete exhumation, but just to explore the general parameters of the site to establish, you know, what we had out there so that we could make plans for, perhaps, further and more detailed investigation later on. So our objectives of that mission was, first, to map the surface features, to examine the features and the surface, for example, as I will point out here a little later on, spent cartridges and other things that would tell us that, perhaps, there had been a mass execution at the site. We also wanted to cut a trench, kind of an exploratory trench, across the site to make sure -- we had these two bodies more or less on the surface, but were there, indeed, more bodies below? Did we have, indeed, a mass grave? Then we also wanted to see whether there was any evidence of disturbance of the site after -- archeologists are pretty good at this, of being able to read the earth -- and had there been any evidence of disturbance of the site from the time the burial was first made, had somebody gone out there and tried to move bodies and things of that sort? Then, finally, to do an examination of the two skeletons that were on the surface. On that mission, I was able to take a short helicopter ride from Vukovar over to circle the site, and this is a view of the scene. The burial or the area we are looking at, exploring or going to explore, is right over in here, up, it is a little hazy but you can see a perimeter of barbed wire rolled, curled wire, around the site which the Russians had placed to keep people out and a sort of a guard shack here that the Russian troops stayed in. They also had sentries posted within a few hundred metres along some of these roads and on further down in the ravine area. So the site had been, apparently, well secured by the Russians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just before you take that off there, Dr. Snow, the trees that you can just protruding into what is my right-hand side of the screen, that is the wooded area that you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right from here on down it is woods, and the further down the ravine you go, the larger the trees. There are some very sizeable trees down there as you go on down toward the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This slide just shows the perimeter here as we arrived. This is Dr. Sanders, Dr. Morris Tidball-Binz and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, if you point on that, I am afraid it will not show up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to point out, you know, I am from Oklahoma we are kind of undeveloped. We are not used to all this sophisticated technology that you people seem to have here, but this is Dr. Sanders, this is Dr. Morris Tidball-Binz, this is myself and another RCMP person who was -- by that time Larry had been rotated home and this gentleman, also a sergeant, had taken over and, unfortunately, I do not recall his name but I can find it for you. But this is the way the site looked as we arrived. This is just another shot of the Russian guard shack out there and one of their vehicles that they used to transport themselves back and forth. Now at this time -- this was in December, mid December -- there had been quite a bit of rain, so the site was essentially about the same except a lot of water had accumulated in there. Since we only had a few days, we had a little engineering problem. We had to develop or dig a drainage ditch to get this surface water out and let it dry out a little bit before we could do much in the way of digging around there. But at that point, though, I did take a walk around into the site to see if there had been any evidence of disturbance or intrusion since I had been there the previous October. I did not find anything except the skull, the skeleton No. 1. Apparently, it had been moved a little bit, and I was curious about that, and I found out later that a British medical officer stationed at Vukovar with the medical detachment there on October 19th, I believe it was, or it could have been October 18th, in the afternoon, had heard about our discovery and had taken it on himself to go out and examine these human remains and, apparently, he picked up the skull and moved it around a little bit, otherwise throughout the area I could see no sign of any disturbance or any intrusion. I did find a vodka bottle -- it looked fairly fresh -- that had been tossed over the wire, I assume by, perhaps, Russian sentries. So at that point we began staking out the site, as we would any other kind of archeological dig. Here you see Dr. Morris Tidball-Binz putting in the stakes and the string. So, with stakes and string, we worked out the area that we felt encompassed the grave a little margin of a metre or so on either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just leaving that there for a moment, how did you determine that, doctor? How was it determined that that would be the approximate perimeters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, you see this sort of open or bald area in here? Now, by this time, by the way, we have cut down the weeds surrounding here with some machetes, so that we would have working space. We had cleared the weeds, the plants around this. One of the features we are talking about a little later on was that, for example, the width of the grave we established at around approximately seven metres from here over to here, and around 10 metres in this direction. Skeleton No. 1, incidentally, is right up in this area, the person that was on the surface there, and skeleton No. 2 away from the main grave, if you went down in this direction and went into these woods here, there is a little trail, and he is about 17 metres lying there, about 17 metres from this corner of the grave. The way we established the approximate width of the grave, for example, is when fill dirt of this sort, you take the dirt out and eventually you put, in this case, bodies but also dirt back in. The dirt that you use for the fill has a different consistency in the structure that is different from the undisturbed soil. With rain and weathering, the grave begins to subside and you will see like fracture lines along the margins of the grave which differentiates the area of undisturbed soil from the area of fill. So, using those fracture lines, we could get at least approximate, pretty close estimates of the original width and length of the grave. Actually, where I said roughly 10 metres for this length in this direction, it is probably a little less accurate than the width, because here it was a little more ambivalent, the soil, so we felt like that, perhaps, the edge of the grave could even come in beyond a string here a little bit, or cord, or even perhaps on the other side of it, but roughly we are talking about an area of disturbed earth seven by 10 metres. Now, as indicated -- let me get you orientated here -- out in this direction, you can just barely see where this man is standing, just beyond him, is the Russian guard shack, the structure. Here is the perimeter. We decided to run our test trench which we made one metre wide across the width of the grave, and here you see some actually UNPROFOR Luxembourg troops -- I think they were attached to BELBAT, but they were a mine clearing group -- and they came out to help us detect metal, we were obviously kind of interested in mines, but also booby traps, but later on even spent cartridges and things of that sort that might suggest that some shooting had gone on out of this site. So, once we set up the perimeter, the trench, they went over it with their equipment. The next stage was removing, beginning to explore the trench here. We, actually some of the Russian troops, sentries, had volunteered to do some of the heavy digging, removing the surface earth. They did a very good job and they were very anxious to work with us. I think by this time they were beginning to get a little bored. They had been out there for a couple of months and maybe a career in archeology was beginning to look more attractive than a military career. But, at any rate, they set to with great enthusiasm. We had them remove the first 10 or 15 centimetres from the top which they could do very rapidly. Once we got down to that depth, though, we slowed down because we began to feel like we were going to be running into evidence of human bodies and, sure enough, we did. For example, here is the boundary, one boundary of the trench, and the other one is not shown in this slide, but here is a human arm -- you can see a sleeve, clothing -- and the hand here lying across this trench. We did not want to expose these people, we knew -- indeed, it was a mass grave -- that we would be encountering human bodies, but at this time we did not want to disturb them any more than we had to because we would, later on we would return and, with a larger crew and better equipment, do a complete exhumation of these bodies. So we would leave them undisturbed. What we did is we worked along this trench. Whenever we came to a body, usually, or a portion of a body, we would go down that far, expose it enough to see what it was, and then we would not under-cut below the body. So, along this trench, however, we found evidence of nine people whose bodies were intersecting and were exposed in that trench. This would be the top layer of bodies in this roughly seven metre long trench. So we felt that that was sufficient evidence at that point to establish that we had a mass grave, and it was not just limited to the two skeletons that we had observed on the surface. In fact, this light probably makes it a little clearer. Here is the trench and you can see at various levels it is kind of stepped, because up in this area a body was very close to the surface, so we worked around him. Then we went down here and we had to go several more centimetres before we found evidence of another body because these are not all in one level. But, in this stretch of trench one metre wide and roughly seven metres long, we could see that there were at least nine bodies exposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the bodies, from your examination of them, all male?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The clothing and the boots, I would have to indicate -- you see, we did not, at this point we were not able to identify or to examine these bodies in detail as we would, but the clothing and the boots suggested, indeed, they were males. We did not see any female clothing. We did not see anything that we would think might belong to children. This is just a rough sketch map of the area, and up in this circular area here is the individual I referred to as skeleton No. 1. The surface skeleton No. 2 will not be shown on this map; he would be back up in this direction out in the sort of wooded area there. Here are the evidence of the margins of, we felt like a bulldozer had been brought in here, well, to dig the grave, and also later on a bulldozer was used to cover up the grave. Now, those marks are a little different than these fracture lines. Here you see the fracture lines I was telling about, where the soil subsided that give us an approximation of the original excavation. Here is our trench going across here and here are indications of some of the bodies that we encountered as we dug that trench.
