I might point out that our archeologist, looking at the soil and the area of disturbance around skeleton No. 1, it was her opinion that he was, perhaps, originally in the grave but pretty close to the surface so that when they closed the grave with the back fill, his body had been, kind of, picked up by the grave and shoved over into this end of the grave in the fill dirt, that perhaps it had been covered sufficiently when the fill was made that no-one noticed that he was very close to the surface and was not completely buried, and that later on weathering and rain had exposed some of the bones to the point where we saw them when we first visited the grave in October 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, does your Honours want to take the adjournment now and resume later because it will be a little bit longer?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. With the agreement of my colleagues, I would agree. I would suggest that we can come back in 15 to 20 minutes time. I did not wish to intervene at this point in the testimony from Dr. Snow, but you, of course, know yourself how many questions you have got and how long it is going to take. So, on that basis I think we could take a break and it would also give the opportunity to the doctor to rest for a short time. So the session is adjourned for 15 to 20 minutes (11.30 p.m.).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, I would like to say on behalf of my colleagues and myself that we have had an interruption which has caused that we had to use some time for something else. We are sorry about this. We can now recommence, we can resume our hearing with the rest of the testimony from Dr. Snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Dr. Snow, could you continue, please, with your evidence in relation to the exhumation, the partial exhumation, that you carried on at the site of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that when we took the recess here, I had been talking about the exploratory trench ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Trench, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that we had made. In addition to that, as I indicated, one of our other objectives was to explore surface features to see if we found any evidence that an execution had occurred or, at least, some shooting had occurred. As it turned out, there was abundant evidence of that around the edges of the grave, in particular, and we found, first, spent cartridges, cartridges without any casings, without any bullets. We even found a few that had not been fired, that apparently had simply dropped. This shows a view of the grave area that we had marked out where a trench was over in this area here, but around the edges of the grave we have -- these little flags show where each approximately we were able to find around 75 spent cartridges still lying on the surface. Now, we did not do any digging or screening so that probably there were many, many more in this vegetation, but these were the ones that we were able to find that were more or less obvious. So we would put a flag to mark them so that we could study the distribution. It was our impression, based on the distribution of these cartridges around the margin of the grave, that perhaps the shooters, the people who were firing, were standing over in this area here, because these cartridges, they were 762 calibre and what I would call AK47, I believe. They will eject to the right and, based on other scenes of this sort that I have investigated in El Savaldor and Kurdistan, particularly, they generally travel maybe as far as 15 to 20 feet. So it was our impression, perhaps, that the shooters were more or less at this corner of the grave and shooting along the trajectory that we see here. We found further evidence of that when we looked at some of the saplings and trees on the far side of the grave at the opposite corner where actually you can see these two gentlemen are putting a probe through a bullet hole that has passed through that limb. We found a number of those and we found bullets embedded in some of the trees in this area. There was also an old rusted metal vehicle in that area just beyond the grave, and it had some bullets embedded in it. So our impression was that there, indeed, had been a number of shots fired in that area and across the grave. Along with that, as I indicated, I wanted to examine as close as I could or in as much detail as I could under field conditions the two skeletons that were obvious on the surface. First, skeleton 1 that was found up right at the -- the first skeleton we encountered right at the edge of the grave area, and the one I said that we thought that, perhaps, during the back filling operation his body had kind of been picked up and moved to that end of the grave and, as I indicated before in my first examination which took place the previous October, I could tell that this individual was, indeed, a male. He was not -- he was an adult male, but I would have to have said his age was in the neighbourhood of 22 to roughly 28 or 9 years of age, and that we did see evidence of a gun shot wound here in the temple and there were some other holes on the other side of the skull that indicated a through and through gun shot wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, were you able to make any assessment of the age of these bodies, having regard to the state of decomposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that always necessarily has to be a pretty broad estimate based on what we could see on the basis of the condition of these two bodies that we could examine in detail and the ones that we saw exposed in the trench, and I felt in my final report I would have to say that probably in the range of, depending on conditions, environmental factors such as climate, rainfall and things of that sort, I would have to say that they had been there at least six months but probably no more than about 18 months, so around a year, plus or minus six months. Now, I continued my examination as well as I could under field conditions and I took some measurements of the bones and made other observations on skeleton 1, so that I could calculate stature and age at death with a certain amount of precision. Actually, I was able also to make a dental chart, he had some dental work. Also, as we examined the clothing that we found around skeleton No. 1 we found around his neck was a, even though it becomes skeletonized, but we could still see that a chain encircled his neck and there were several small objects on that chain. Here is a close-up of what we saw. It is a crucifix here. This, apparently, is a common little gold, little good luck charm, and over here is a medallion, a metal medallion, and translated it says, "God and Croatia". We understood, we were told, that these sorts of medals were often worn by the Croatian military, paramilitary soldiers. The cross is a Roman Catholic ornament, so we felt that was, at least, minimal evidence that this person, based on the effects found with him, was Croatian. Now, turning to the second skeleton, the one that we found away from the site, we found quite a bit of clothing from him and also, despite the fact that some of the bones had been damaged by animals, I was able to take enough measurements to get again an age estimate, stature, a few features like that, that could tell us about this individual, and also a very, even though it was under field conditions, a pretty good dental chart. For example, here are the bones of his pelvis, the hip bones and the sacrum, part of the lower part of the spine, that I was able -- they were disarticulated but able more or less to fit them together, and the configuration of this pelvis is definitely male and there were also some morphological features on the pubic bones, which are the front part of the hip bones here, that gave us a pretty reliable age indicator so I could come up with an age estimate of this individual; also in his 20s. Also some of his clothing -- this is one garment that says, "Canadian", and I can no longer recall exactly what, but there was English here, and there was at least one other garment that suggested that they came from Canada. Now, later on I was told that during the siege of Vukovar a Canadian relief organisation, maybe an organisation of Canadian Croatians, had taken up collections of old clothing to send to the people of Vukovar, and that this clothing was primarily distributed to patients in the hospital. So I thought that these garments that suggested a Canadian connection at least suggested that, perhaps, we were dealing with a person who had obtained clothing donated by Canadians there at Vukovar Hospital. Finally, in a pocket of one of his garments we found this little medallion, either St. Joseph, I believe, and again a Roman Catholic piece of religious art that might be kept by a person; also suggesting, therefore, that the victim was Catholic, Roman Catholic, as opposed to Serb. Finally, on the third day of our work, we went ahead and we took the two skeletons that were -- the surface skeletons, and after my examination we bagged them separately and as we closed this trench we put them here right at the end of the trench with their labels, so that when and if eventually the grave is completely excavated, we will be able to return and identify those two skeletons. We will know that they will be the ones in the plastic bags at the end of this trench so they can be removed for further examination. We closed up the trench and left the site more or less in the condition as you see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, as far as you know, has any further exhumation work been carried out on this grave since the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at this point. Later on in March of, it would have been '93, I returned with Mr. Eric Stover and Commander Fenrick who at that time was part of the commission of experts, and we went out to the site and looked at it from the perimeter. We did not go into the grave area. In fact, it gave me some confidence in that the Russians, the guards were doing their job because they would not allow either myself or Major or Commander Fenrick or any of our party to go in beyond the wire. So, we left at that time, after I was able to point out most of the features to Commander Fenrick and his assistant. Then, as you may be aware, later that year, in fact in November of that year, we mounted I guess what I would call an expedition, including several archeologists from the United States, my colleague Dr. Bill Hagland, and several multinational team -- I had people I had worked with and helped trained in Argentina and Guatemala and Chile joining us -- and it was our intention and we thought arrangements had been made to go out and actually do a thorough exhumation at the site. In fact, we were -- the team was deployed at the site ready to begin work when the Serb local authorities indicated that they would not permit any further investigation of the site at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know which particular branch of the Serb administration obstructed your further exhumation work out there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got the impression, I had stayed back over Pakrac -- we were looking at another grave there -- but I believe it was, if I am not mistaken, it may have been the Vukovar City Council or the local people in the Vukovar area, whatever the governmental administration. It had been my understanding that the people up in Knin, at the seat of the government, had given clearance for this exhumation, but that the local people overrode that decision. So our team had to redeploy to another site. So, to that point I do not believe there has been any other disturbance or any investigation at Vukovar. So the scene should be just about as it was left in December, on December 19th, around 11 o'clock in the morning as I showed in that last slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, I think you may have said this but, just for the sake of clarification, when you arrived at the scene either on the first occasion in October '92 or the later occasion in December '92, were you able to make any assessment of whether or not, in your opinion, the grave had been disturbed from the time of the execution and internment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we saw no evidence of that and on the second trip our archeologist, Dr. Rebecca Saunders, looked at that very carefully from that standpoint, to see whether there was any evidence of any secondary disturbance like someone could have come in a few months later, a few weeks later, and had done some work or disturbed the site, and there was nothing that would indicate that. So, it was our opinion that whenever that grave was made there was no, which based on the vegetation, we felt like it was about a year prior to the discovery of the site, that there was no major disturbance -- intrusion or .....

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, based on your previous experiences in these matters and having regard to the dimensions of the grave that you were able to map out when you were on the site, are you able to make any estimate of its capacity in terms of how many people could be fitted into the grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a rough indicator based on what we know -- the volume of the human body, the space that it occupies, even with clothing and shoes, footwear, things of that sort, it is rather easy to get as many as five, easily five, bodies into a cubic metre of space. That always seems remarkable to people, but there would be room left over. Based on the dimensions of this grave, we are talking about roughly, as I said before, around seven to 10 metres, which is not a very big space, Hamlet's wound -- it is not as wide as a barn and deep as a well but it is sufficient -- and in that seven by 10 metre space, assuming that we have a depth of at least a metre, it is a matter of simple arithmetic, seven times 10 would be roughly 70, and multiply that by five to get the vertical dimension, so we could get 350 bodies in that grave -- at least. At this point, though, all we can say is that we saw evidence of nine bodies, the two on the surface -- excuse me, eleven bodies; the two on the surface and the nine that were exposed in our trenching effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, I would ask now that we tender the map that you first referred to, exhibit 28, Prosecution exhibit 28. Doctor, I understand that the slides that you have just taken us through are the only copies in existence of those slides, but you have agreed that they will be made available for us for the purposes of copying so that they may subsequently be tendered as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions of the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Odio Benito, Judge Riad? Doctor, could I ask you an additional question? How would you -- the Prosecutor might have something to say about my question as well -- explain this relative degree of negligence on the part of local authorities regarding this site? About a year or 18 months went by and nobody did anything about this location. You have some experience in the former Yugoslavia and, on that basis, will you conclude that that negligence was characteristic of other sites in that country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would have to say so because, as I understand it, no, I have not been down to the other graves that are being located in Bosnia, but the reports that I read that very often at these graves human remains are visible on the surface. But this kind of I guess you would say negligence, you know, is not particularly confined to Yugoslavia, because I have seen in other countries where people have not been too careful in covering up clandestine graves. Maybe, I do not know, perhaps, you know, they feel like: "Well, we do not have to worry about it because we are going to be in control here for ever and there is not going to be anybody around to look at it", but sometimes they are wanting in the dismal technology of trying to bury people.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like now to ask the prosecuting counsel: within the context of this present indictment, have your investigators, physically speaking, visited this particular location where this mass grave is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, some representatives of the office have been to the grave site, your Honour. The grave site is not readily accessible, I should say. It is at the moment under the control of UNTAES but it is still, if I say so ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Under whose control? Would you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- (inaudible) control but actually it is still Serb held territory, so access to it is not terribly easy. Hence, the reason why the exhumation could not proceed when it was planned.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much counsel for the Prosecution. We have no further questions. Doctor, the Tribunal would like to acknowledge very much your testimony and also it appreciates the discipline and also the calmness and serenity with which you have given your testimony. It is no doubt due to your great experience, as the Prosecutor has said. Quite clearly, we have to keep all the elements which you personally have been able to gather together and make them available to the Prosecution, but the Prosecutor has already talked about that. The Tribunal would like to thank you and wish you a good trip back. Thank you very much. Would you show the witness out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. That concludes the evidence that we wish to call in these proceedings. At this stage, if your Honours permit, or at some subsequent stage, my colleague, Mr. Williamson, would wish to address you on the evidence that has been presented.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecutor Williamson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the indictment that is before you charges three individuals with grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, violations of the Laws or Customs of War and Crimes Against Humanity. At this point I would like to reaffirm the position set forth by Mr. Niemann at the outset of this hearing, that the Prosecutor maintains that all of these charges are cumulative, but also that this an issue that need not be addressed in a hearing of this nature. Rather, it is an issue that should be resolved at the trial stage and then, as Mr. Niemann suggested, perhaps only at the point that sentences were to be imposed. In regard to the substance of the charges alleged in the indictment, however, you have heard over the past week the testimony of eleven witnesses. You have seen video footage taken largely from Serbian cameras and broadcast on Belgrade television. You have seen Vukovar before the war, an attractive city which had grown up over hundreds of years on the banks of the Danube; a city that had existed for centuries but which was virtually destroyed in just over three months by an army that claimed to be liberating it. This army many employed every weapon in their arsenal: artillery, rockets, aircraft, naval gunboats and over 30,000 troops to defeat a lightly armed Croatian force of around 1800 men. The military victory and destruction of the city were not enough, because it was when this victory was achieved that the true horror began. On 19th November 1991 the JNA had crushed the Croatian resistance in most Vukovar. Fighting still continued in the Mitnica area on the southeast side of the city, but in the centre of the town the fighting had come to an end. As the JNA and their paramilitary allies moved in to occupy the city, civilians began crawling out of the cellars where they had stayed for the last three months. After all that they had survived, apparently many of them were to be shot down as they came out, and many more were killed before they even left the cellars. Fearing just this sort of bloodbath, hundreds of people had taken refuge at the hospital, believing it to be a place of safety. By the afternoon of 19th when the first JNA soldiers arrived at the hospital, there were probably more than a thousand civilians gathered in and around what was left of the hospital building. Many of the soldiers who had fought to defend Vukovar had also come there. Only a few of them were professional soldiers. Most were just men who lived in the city and had taken up arms to defend their homes when the fighting began. Some had come to the hospital during the course of the battle because they had been wounded. Others had gone there in the closing days of the battle having heard that the hospital would be evacuated in the presence of international observers. By all accounts, these men had already put down their arms and no one offered resistance to the JNA soldiers who came to the hospital. Dr. Bosanac and her staff who had continued to work under appalling conditions for three months, grew worried when the international monitors had not arrived. They had in fact arrived. An ECMM team, which included Dr. Jan Schou, was in Negoslavci, only 3 kilometres away from Vukovar and the hospital. They had reached the JNA headquarters there and were fully prepared to go on to the hospital that day, but they were blocked by Colonel Mrksic and Major Sljivancanin who would not allow it, saying that it was not safe to go there. That night a Red Cross team did reach the hospital, but Sljivancanin had them thrown out. Finally an agreement was reached that the ECMM and the Red Cross would go in the following morning, the 20th of November. On that day the monitors got up and departed fairly early in the morning, around, 8 or 9. Before they could get to the hospital, though, events there were already unfolding very quickly. Major Sljivancanin had summoned all of the hospital staff to a meeting around 7 in the morning. While he preached to the doctors about how he had liberated Vukovar, his soldiers were hurriedly rounding up all of the fighting age men, which in their eyes included boys as young as 16 and men as old as 76. They forced them out a back door and into the hospital yard. All of these men were unarmed, many were wounded, pulled out of their hospital beds. As this process was ongoing, Dr. Schou and his ECMM team as well the Red Cross representative were approaching the hospital. Before they could get there, though, Major Sljivancanin appears again, this time on the bridge over the Vuka River only a few blocks from the hospital. Claiming that it is not safe for them to proceed, he and his soldiers detained the ECMM and the Red Cross for over two hours. As Belgrade television films away, Sljivancanin screams at the Red Cross representative who dares insist that he live up to an agreement signed by his own army. In this two-hour period, though, the fate of the 260 or so men was being sealed. They had been taken outside the building and searched by the JNA soldiers. They were loaded on to buses parked on Gunduliceva Street and then they were driven to the JNA barracks under guard. By the time the ECMM, the Red Cross and Cyrus Vance got to the hospital, these men and boys were already being driven away, most of them to their deaths. When they arrived at the barracks they found a number of Serb irregulars, or Chetniks as they were called, waiting for them. As the men remained seated on the buses, these Chetniks walked around the buses brandishing their weapons yelling threats at them. Some of them even got on the buses to reinforce the threats, but this was not the place where they were to be carried out. While at the barracks Captain Radic got on each of the buses and read out a list of names. Apparently, the men on the list were either related to hospital staff or were staff members themselves. They were taken off of the buses and put into another vehicle for transport back to the hospital. All of the other men remained on the buses, though, waiting and listening to the threats being shouted at them. After about two hours the buses left again and begin travelling south in the direction of Negoslavci. About a kilometre south of Vukovar the buses turned left on a road through the fields and leading to the Ovcara farm complex. When the buses arrived at Ovcara they turned in front of the main building which has been described as a hangar. As each bus pulled up the men were made to get off and run through a gauntlet of Serb paramilitary and JNA soldiers. These troops beat the men with fists, with clubs, with rifle butts. They stripped their coats and hats off them, took their documents, watches and jewellery. Once the victims survived this round of abuse, they were gathered inside the hangar where the beatings continued and intensified. The so-called Chetniks as well as JNA soldiers hit and kicked the men over the next few hours. At least two men died there in the hangar as a result of the beatings. While this was going on about seven men were pulled out of the hangar by Serbs who knew them from before or chose for one reason or another to intervene on their behalf. During this hearing you have heard from three of those men. As for the other two 260 or so men who were in the hangar, none of the paramilitary troops or JNA soldiers stepped forward to save them. They were consigned to death. After the lucky seven were driven away back to Vukovar, the remaining men were registered by the JNA, and shortly thereafter they were divided into small groups of 10 to 20 men. An army truck with a canvas cover on the back was brought up to the building and the first group of men was loaded into this truck. It drove away and then returned about 15 minutes later and the next group of men was put in. As we know from the testimony of Witness B who was in the fourth or fifth group put in the truck, it left the hangar and travelled south on the road toward Grabovo. Less than a kilometre from the hangar the truck turned left at a dip in the road and then drove along a wooded ravine. Witness B at that point jumped out and was able to get away. Not far from the place where he jumped the small road ended at the head of this ravine. At this location the men were taken out of the truck and there they were brutally murdered. As Dr. Snow told you, there were numerous spent cartridges found on the ground where the shooters had fired their weapons. On the opposite side of the site the trees bore scars from the bullets. In between the men fell and there they were shoved into a mass grave, a grave that had been prepared by the bulldozer that Witness K had heard as he stood outside the Ovcara hangar. Some were not buried well enough, though, and their bodies were there for Dr. Snow to filed almost a year later. One of them, as you saw, with a very prominent bullet hole in the front of his skull. Even in the preliminary findings of Dr. Snow, there is strong evidence that the men in this grave were Croatian and that they came from the hospital. Your Honours, these killings did not happen by chance. This was a well orchestrated, very organised event. Amid the chaos that was Vukovar on 20th November 1991, the JNA made sure of one thing and that was that this mass execution was going to take place. The two highest ranking JNA officers in Vukovar, Colonel Mrksic and Major Sljivancanin, dedicated all of their efforts to ensure that it did. Sljivancanin's trusted subordinate, Captain Radic, assisted them at every turn. I would submit that the evidence against these three individuals is substantial. Colonel Mrksic was the commander of the Guards Brigade, the JNA unit with responsibility for the occupation of the city. As Witness A told you, nothing happened in Vukovar without his knowledge and approval. When Dr. Bosanac became worried that no international observers had arrived at the hospital, she contacted the Croatian government and both they and General Raseta, the official JNA negotiator, told her that Colonel Mrksic had responsibility for the hospital's evacuation. When Dr. Bosanac spoke directly with Mrksic, he indicated that he was aware of the agreement to evacuate the hospital in the presence of international monitors, but he said that it was no longer possible. He said this despite the fact that ECMM and ICRC representatives were already in his very same headquarters and were asking to go to the hospital. Dr. Bosanac even attempted to speak with them, but Mrksic would not permit it. His superiors said he was responsible for the hospital. He acknowledged his responsibility, and he had the power to ensure that the evacuation was done properly, but instead he did everything he would could to see to it that his subordinates were able to carry out this crime undetected. Captain Radic, the commander of the Special Infantry Company within the Guards Brigade, was a close associate of Sljivancanin. He worked side by side with him throughout the battle, and he is with him again on 20th November at the hospital. It is he that Sljivancanin entrusts with searching the men taken from the hospital and it is Radic that Sljivancanin sends to the JNA barracks to retrieve the men that were not supposed to end up at Ovcara. The night of the murders, he is back at his headquarters as soldiers in his company laugh and boast of the killings, yet he takes no action against them. His friend, Major Sljivancanin, is the man who makes this all happen. He is clearly the officer in charge at the hospital itself. As he occupies the entire staff in a meeting, his soldiers are forcing the male patients outside. He orders Radic to search them and then he sends them on to the buses. He personally blocks the ECMM, the Red Cross and the UN envoy from reaching the hospital. He clearly knows the fate intended for the men, because he takes action to save some of them, a task he assigns to Radic. The others, though, are sent on to Ovcara under the guard of Sljivancanin's soldiers. But despite their efforts to perpetrate the perfect crime, there were flaws because they did not count on the fact that among these horrific murderers there would be a few who still had a shred of human decency about them. And these few, very few apparently, would let seven men leave Ovcara alive. Some of these men, as well as the one man able to escape from the death truck, have come before you and told this tragic story. As to the specific charges set forth in the indictment, the accused are all charged with Grave Breaches of the Geneva Conventions under Article 2 of our Statute; Violations of the Laws or Customs of War under Article 3, and Crimes Against Humanity under Article 5. In order for any or all of these to be applicable, there must exist a state of armed conflict. The evidence is clear that this was the case in Croatia and in Vukovar in particular on 20th November 1991. With respect to Article 2, the conflict must be shown to have been international in character and that the victims were persons protected by the Geneva Conventions. As Dr. Gow indicated in his testimony, Croatia had declared its independence in June 1991 and, although this was initially suspended at the request of the International Community, it did become effective in October 1991, well before the events at issue in this case. This was a war waged by the Government of Yugoslavia in Belgrade against an independent Croatia, thus a war between two sovereign states; in other words, international. As to Article 3 charges, the Prosecutor must show that the act or omission charged is a violation of the laws or customs of war. In this instance, the accused are charged with cruel treatment and murder, both of which are violations of the minimum rules applicable to all armed conflicts, as is made evident by the listing and description of such acts within Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. With respect to Article 5, the acts of the accused must have been knowingly committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against a civilian population. This has had been established here in several ways. First, by the testimony of Dr. Gow who provided the court with a perspective on the wide-ranging attack by the JNA on several fronts in Croatia. Secondly, you have heard the testimony of several persons who have described the forces arrayed against the city of Vukovar and the manner in which those forces were utilized to totally destroy the city and to kill well over a thousand civilians. Finally, you have heard testimony related to this incident alone which has shown that well over 200 men were murdered, some of them young boys, some elderly and incapacitated. The scope of this mass murder taken alone should be sufficient to constitute a widespread and systematic attack. The three accused may not have pulled the triggers on the guns that killed the 260 or so men, but they did everything they could to see that this crime was executed. Under either Article 7(1) as perpetrators individually responsible for these acts, or under Article 7(3) as commanders responsible for the acts of their subordinates, there is ample evidence of culpability. In light of this evidence that has been presented to you, the Prosecutor requests that you make a determination that reasonable grounds exist for believing that the accused have committed all or any of the crimes charged in the indictment, and that you order accordingly the issuance of international arrest warrants for all three. Your Honours, my co-counsel, Mr. Niemann, told you in this his opening statement that the seeds of genocide were laid in Vukovar and, indeed, they were. On the video tape you heard Major Sljivancanin tell Cyrus Vance that this is a dirty war, but it is he who chose that path. It is he and his fellow officers that chose to employ murder as a weapon of the Yugoslav Army. On 20th November 1991 it is they who set the precedent, a precedent of mass murder which has been repeated again and again over the past four years in Croatia and Bosnia alike. It is both fascinating and horrifying to watch the film of these men as the events unfold. They are proud, they are arrogant, as more than one witness has told you, but it is hard to imagine what they are so proud of. They are not fighting valiantly on a field of battle; they are not overcoming a well-armed foe. Instead, they are taking unarmed men, many of them wounded, dragged out of hospital beds. They have been beaten unmercifully for hours and then they have been murdered in cold blood. These are not the acts of brave warriors. These are the acts of cowards, cowards who choose the vulnerable and the defenceless as their victims. They are the acts of criminals. Where are these proud men today? Today they hide. They hide behind the shelter of the government that sent them there and that still seeks to protect them. That government, the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, has been informed of the indictments against them. The official records of the Tribunal Registry document that the indictment in this matter was confirmed by Judge Riad on the 7th of November 1995. On the following day arrest warrants directed to the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Belgrade were hand delivered to the Yugoslav Embassy here in The Hague. When no action was taken by the Yugoslav government to act on those warrants, the Prosecutor sought, in accordance with Rules 60 and 61, to have newspaper advertisements published in Yugoslavia to notify the accused of the indictments. This request was will also transmitted to the Yugoslav Embassy in The Hague on the 23rd of January 1996. Yet the government does nothing. They can arrest them at any time, but they do not. In this case, the accused are all citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and are known to be on its territory either in Serbia or Montenegro. After Vukovar the government gave them commendations and promotions. In the case of at least one of them, Major Sljivancanin, he is a still serving officer in the Yugoslav Army with an obligation to obey orders given to him by that government. They can compel him to report where they choose. Recent news report from Belgrade even indicate that he is now assigned to the Yugoslav Military Academy situated in Belgrade, the seat of the government. They have promoted, supported and continued to pay an indicted war criminal, and to maintain him as a senior officer in their army. If these reports are correct, they now even have him training officer cadets. Can there be any more flagrant way of showing their disregard and even contempt for their obligations as a Member State of the United Nations, obligations they recently re-affirmed by entering into the Dayton Accords. In this case it is very clear that the failure to effect personal service on the accused and to secure their arrests and transfer to The Hague, is due solely to the refusal of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to co-operate with the Tribunal as it is required to do. When a government gives refuge and support to criminals, in the eyes of the world, that government then too becomes criminal, and that is exactly what the Belgrade government has done in this case. It is, therefore, the request of the Prosecutor that in addition to the issuance of international arrest warrants, this Chamber should also certify to the President of the Tribunal that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has failed to comply with its obligations under Article 29 of the Statute, and further recommend to the President that he notify the Security Council of this refusal to co-operate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, that brings the hearing to an end. The Chamber will issue its decision on Wednesday, 3rd April at 9.30. The session is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: (The hearing adjourned for a short time)
